senses.definition: Hard to understand because it is deeply complex or theoretical.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'abtrusus', meaning hidden away or concealed. English developed the sense of something mentally hidden from easy understanding.

senses.definition: The special way a person or group pronounces words.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'accentus', meaning song added to speech or tone of voice. In English, the meaning expanded to include stress in words and the characteristic pronunciation of a speaker or group.

senses.definition: Sharp, harsh, and biting in tone or style.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'acerbus', meaning bitter or harsh. English first used it literally for sourness and then figuratively for sharp language.

senses.definition: The small nut of an oak tree.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'æcern', which originally could refer more broadly to tree fruit or mast. In English, the meaning narrowed over time to the nut of the oak tree.

senses.definition: To respect or like someone or something very much.

history.etymology_note: English 'admire' came through Old French from Latin 'admirari', meaning to wonder at. Over time, the meaning softened from amazement toward strong respect or approval.

senses.definition: Skillful, quick, and clever in action or thought.

history.etymology_note: Borrowed from French 'adroit', meaning skillful or dexterous, originally tied to the right hand. English uses it for clever practical skill.

senses.definition: Friendly, approachable, and easy to speak with.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'affabilis', meaning easy to speak to, from a verb meaning to address or speak to. English uses it for warm and approachable friendliness.

senses.definition: Feeling fear or worry about something.

history.etymology_note: English 'afraid' came through forms related to fear and sudden fright in Old French. It became the everyday English word for feeling fear.

senses.definition: Eager and cheerful readiness to act.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'alacritas', meaning liveliness or eagerness. English uses it for brisk, willing enthusiasm.

senses.definition: Quick to notice and ready to respond.

history.etymology_note: From Italian 'all'erta', meaning on the watch or on guard. English uses it for wakeful attention and readiness.

senses.definition: To examine something carefully in order to understand it better.

history.etymology_note: From Greek analyein, meaning to unloose or break up, from ana- (up) + lyein (to loosen). First used in logic and science to describe breaking a subject into parts.

senses.definition: A heavy metal device dropped from a ship to the sea floor to keep the ship from drifting.

history.etymology_note: From Latin ancora, from Greek ankura, meaning hook or anchor. The hook shape of the anchor gives it its name.

senses.definition: Very old and from a long time ago.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'ancien', meaning former or old, from Latin roots connected with what comes before. English uses it for distant historical times and very old things.

senses.definition: Feeling strong displeasure because something feels unfair, hurtful, or wrong.

history.etymology_note: English 'angry' comes from Old Norse 'angr', meaning grief or sorrow. In English, it developed into the common word for strong upset or anger.

senses.definition: A very small insect that lives in underground colonies and works together with others.

history.etymology_note: From Old English æmette, meaning ant or emmet. The modern shortened form developed in Middle English.

senses.definition: The study of human beings, including their cultures, societies, and physical development.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἀνθρωπολογία' (anthropologia), built from words meaning human and study. In English, it came to mean the scientific study of humans and human cultures.

senses.definition: A lack of interest, feeling, or care about what happens.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἀπάθεια' (apatheia), meaning absence of feeling or freedom from passion, through Latin forms. In English, it came to mean indifference or lack of caring.

senses.definition: A round fruit with red, green, or yellow skin and a crisp inside.

history.etymology_note: Derived from the Proto-Germanic 'aplaz', it is one of the oldest fruit names in the English language.

senses.definition: A cloth worn over the front of the body to keep clothes clean.

history.etymology_note: English 'apron' came from an earlier form 'napron', from Old French 'naperon', meaning a small cloth. The initial 'n' was later lost through a common redivision in speech.

senses.definition: Known or understood by only a small number of people.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'arcanus', meaning secret or hidden, from 'arca', chest or box. English uses it for rare, specialized, or secret knowledge.

senses.definition: The study of past human life through objects, buildings, and other remains left behind.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἀρχαιολογία' (archaiologia), meaning discussion of ancient things, through Latin and French forms. In modern English, it narrowed to the scientific study of the human past through material remains.

senses.definition: Very dry, with little or no rain.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'aridus', meaning dry or parched. English uses it especially for deserts, regions, and climates with very little moisture.

senses.definition: Acting as if you are better or more important than other people.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'arrogans', meaning claiming too much for oneself, from 'arrogare', to claim. English uses it for overconfident pride and superiority.

senses.definition: Creative work made to express ideas, feelings, or beauty.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'ars', meaning skill, craft, or method, through Old French forms. English kept both the sense of practiced skill and the creative sense of artistic work.

senses.definition: Able to express thoughts clearly and effectively in speech or writing.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'articulatus', meaning divided into joints or distinct parts, from 'articulus', joint. English extended that idea to speech that is clear and distinctly formed.

senses.definition: Feeling bad because you think you did something wrong or embarrassing.

history.etymology_note: Built from English words for shame and the state of feeling it. English uses it for the feeling of guilt, embarrassment, or disgrace.

senses.definition: Showing steady, careful, and persistent effort.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'assiduus', meaning constant or busy. English uses it for sustained diligence and careful effort.

senses.definition: Quick to notice important details and make smart judgments.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'astus', meaning craft or cleverness, through French forms. In English, it came to describe sharp, practical intelligence.

senses.definition: The layer of air and gases that surrounds a planet.

history.etymology_note: Coined from Greek atmos (vapor) + sphaira (sphere). First used in scientific writing in the 1600s to describe the envelope of air around the earth.

senses.definition: A very tiny unit of an element that forms all ordinary matter.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἄτομος' (atomos), meaning indivisible, through Latin forms. The ancient idea changed over time, but the word remains central in modern chemistry and physics.

senses.definition: A steady state in which different parts are even or work well together.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'balance', meaning scales for weighing, from Latin forms about a two-pan scale. The word later broadened from weighing devices to the idea of steadiness and evenness.

senses.definition: A round object used in many sports and games.

history.etymology_note: From Old Norse böllr, meaning a round object. Replaced the Old English beall in Middle English as a common word for spherical objects.

senses.definition: A thin rubber bag filled with air or gas that floats or can be tied as a decoration.

history.etymology_note: From French ballon, an augmentative of balle (ball), from Italian ballone. First used to describe large air-filled spheres used for flight.

senses.definition: The tough outer covering of a tree trunk or branch.

history.etymology_note: This tree word entered English from a Scandinavian source such as Old Norse 'börkr'. It replaced the older native English word 'rind' in many uses.

senses.definition: A light or signal that helps guide or warn people.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'bēacen', meaning a sign, signal, or lighthouse-like marker. The word has long carried the idea of guidance or warning.

senses.definition: A large, heavy wild animal with thick fur and a short tail.

history.etymology_note: From Old English bera, a very ancient Germanic word for bear. Many cultures avoided saying the bear's real name, fearing it would summon the animal.

senses.definition: A flying insect with yellow and black stripes that makes honey and can sting.

history.etymology_note: From Old English bēo, one of the oldest insect words in the language, with roots in Proto-Germanic *bijō.

senses.definition: Kind and well-meaning in a way that seeks to help others.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'benevolens', meaning wishing well, from 'bene', well, and 'velle', to wish. English uses it for active goodwill and kindness.

senses.definition: Gentle, harmless, and not likely to cause injury or trouble.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'benignus', meaning kind or favorable. English uses it both for gentle personal qualities and for harmless medical conditions.

senses.definition: The scientific study of living things like plants, animals, and humans.

history.etymology_note: Formed from Greek 'βίος' (bios) meaning life, and '-logia' meaning study. It became the blanket term for the life sciences.

senses.definition: A warm-blooded animal with feathers, two wings, and a beak.

history.etymology_note: From Old English bridd, originally meaning a baby bird or nestling. The modern sense of any bird developed over time.

senses.definition: To grow flowers or to open into flower.

history.etymology_note: English 'bloom' came from a Scandinavian source related to Old Norse 'blómi', meaning flower or blossom. It has remained a core word for flowering and thriving.

senses.definition: Not sharp, or very direct in speech.

history.etymology_note: The word likely came into English from a Scandinavian source related to dullness or a rounded end. English kept both the physical sense of not being sharp and the figurative sense of directness.

senses.definition: Talking too proudly about yourself or what you have done.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'boast', which came into English through older Germanic and French-influenced forms meaning proud talk or bragging. The adjective means full of bragging.

senses.definition: A collection of printed pages bound together for reading.

history.etymology_note: From Old English bōc, originally meaning beech tree, as early writings were carved into beech wood tablets.

senses.definition: Rude, rough, and lacking good manners.

history.etymology_note: From Dutch 'boer', meaning farmer or peasant, through an older social stereotype of rough country manners. English uses it for behavior that is crude or impolite.

senses.definition: Feeling tired of something because it is not interesting.

history.etymology_note: The emotional sense grew from the English verb 'bore', meaning to weary or tire someone. English uses 'bored' for lacking interest or engagement.

senses.definition: The front part of a boat.

history.etymology_note: The ship term is related to Old English 'bōg', meaning shoulder or curved arm. It was applied to the curved forward part of a vessel.

senses.definition: Ready to face something hard or scary without giving up.

history.etymology_note: English 'brave' came through French, where it described bold or valiant qualities. It became a common word in English for courage.

senses.definition: Quick, active, and full of energy.

history.etymology_note: English 'brisk' likely came through French-related forms associated with lively or sharp movement. It came to mean energetic quickness in action or manner.

senses.definition: Wide from side to side.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'brād', meaning wide or open. The word is inherited from Germanic and has stayed close to its original meaning.

senses.definition: A small stream of flowing water.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'broc', meaning a flowing stream. Its deeper origin is uncertain, but the English meaning has stayed close to a small natural waterway.

senses.definition: An insect with large, colorful wings that starts life as a caterpillar.

history.etymology_note: From Old English buttorfleoge, meaning butter-fly. The origin of the butter connection is debated — possibly named for yellow butter-colored varieties.

senses.definition: Extremely complicated, intricate, and hard to follow.

history.etymology_note: The word comes from Byzantium, the ancient Greek name of Constantinople, later the center of the Byzantine Empire. English developed the figurative sense of overwhelming complexity from associations with Byzantine politics, ceremony, and administration.

senses.definition: A small room or covered space inside a boat.

history.etymology_note: English 'cabin' came through Old French 'cabane', meaning a small hut or shelter. It later became a common word for small rooms on ships.

senses.definition: A sweet baked food made from flour, sugar, eggs, and butter.

history.etymology_note: From Old Norse kaka, meaning a cake or flat bread. Entered English and became distinct from bread to specifically mean sweetened baked goods.

senses.definition: A young cow or other large grazing animal.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'cealf', meaning calf. It is a core Germanic farm word with the same basic meaning in modern English.

senses.definition: Feeling or showing little care about other people's pain.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'callosus', meaning hard-skinned or thickened. English first used it for hardened skin and later for emotional hard-heartedness.

senses.definition: Peaceful and not upset, angry, or excited.

history.etymology_note: The word came into English through Romance forms ultimately linked to Greek 'καῦμα' (kauma), meaning heat or hot weather calm. English developed the broader sense of stillness and emotional peace.

senses.definition: A device used to capture photographs or record videos.

history.etymology_note: From the Latin phrase camera obscura meaning dark chamber, describing the optical device that preceded cameras. The modern photographic camera was invented in 1839.

senses.definition: A stick of wax with a wick that gives light when it burns.

history.etymology_note: English 'candle' came through Old English 'candel', borrowed from Latin 'candela'. The Latin word is related to 'candere', meaning to shine.

senses.definition: The quality of being open, honest, and straightforward.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'candor', meaning brightness or whiteness, later associated with openness and purity. English uses it for frank honesty in speech or attitude.

senses.definition: A deep, narrow valley with steep sides, often cut by a river.

history.etymology_note: English 'canyon' came from Mexican Spanish 'cañon'. In that form, the word was used for a deep gorge or hollow, and English adopted it for the landform.

senses.definition: Changing suddenly and unpredictably in mood, choice, or behavior.

history.etymology_note: From Italian 'capriccioso', meaning whimsical or sudden in change, from 'capriccio'. English uses it for unpredictability in decisions, feelings, or conduct.

senses.definition: The person in charge of a boat or ship.

history.etymology_note: English 'captain' came through Old French from Late Latin 'capitaneus', meaning chief or leader. It became the standard word for the person commanding a vessel.

senses.definition: To feel concern for someone or something and want to help or protect it.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'carian', meaning to care, be anxious, or feel concern. English uses it for concern, affection, and protection.

senses.definition: Not giving enough attention or thought to what should be done.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'care', from Old English 'caru', plus the suffix '-less'. English uses it for lacking proper concern, caution, or attention.

senses.definition: Showing kindness, concern, and a wish to help others.

history.etymology_note: Built from English 'care', from Old English 'caru', meaning sorrow, concern, or attentive thought. The adjective developed the positive sense of showing concern in a helpful way.

senses.definition: A large stone fortress built in the Middle Ages to protect a king or queen.

history.etymology_note: From Norman French castel, from Latin castellum (fortified place), a diminutive of castrum (fort). The word entered Old English via the Norman Conquest.

senses.definition: A small, soft-furred animal kept as a pet that purrs and meows.

history.etymology_note: From Old English catt, derived from Late Latin cattus. Cats were domesticated in ancient Egypt and the word spread as cats traveled with traders.

senses.definition: Sharply critical in a way that wounds or burns like acid.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'καυστικός' (kaustikos), meaning able to burn, through Latin and French forms. English uses it literally for corrosive substances and figuratively for cutting criticism.

senses.definition: Careful to avoid danger or mistakes.

history.etymology_note: English 'cautious' was formed from 'caution' and the suffix '-ous', and it reflects the Latin adjective 'cautus', meaning careful or heedful. The word has kept that meaning of careful watchfulness.

senses.definition: A person who wins first place in a competition or fights for a cause.

history.etymology_note: From Old French champion, meaning a fighter who represented another in combat, derived from Late Latin campio (fighter in the field).

senses.definition: One main section of a book.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'chapitre', from Late Latin 'capitulum', literally meaning 'little head'. It came to mean a main heading or division in a book.

senses.definition: The kind of person someone is shown by their actions, values, and habits.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'χαρακτήρ' (charakter), meaning an engraved mark or distinctive sign, through Latin and French forms. English developed the moral sense of a person's inner qualities and stable traits.

senses.definition: Generous and willing to help people in need.

history.etymology_note: The word developed through Old French and English from Late Latin 'caritas', meaning love or generosity. English uses it for giving help and for kindly judgment toward others.

senses.definition: The science that studies what substances are made of and how they combine and change.

history.etymology_note: Derived from 'alchemy', which traces back through Arabic 'al-kimiya' to Greek 'chemeia'. The modern English term refers to the empirical, scientific study of matter.

senses.definition: The part of a song that repeats, often with the same words each time.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'khoros' through Latin 'chorus'. The word first referred to a group that sang or danced together before it developed the modern song meaning.

senses.definition: In Greek thought and myth, Chronos is a figure or name connected with time.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'χρόνος' (chronos), meaning time. In later Greek and European tradition, the word was also treated as the name of a personified figure of time, distinct from the Titan Cronus.

senses.definition: Polite and respectful behavior, especially when people disagree.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'civilitas', meaning courtesy or conduct proper to a citizen, through French forms. English uses it for respectful social behavior and public manners.

senses.definition: A high, steep face of rock or earth.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'clif', meaning a steep slope, bank, or cliff. The word is inherited from early Germanic and remains a basic landform term.

senses.definition: The usual pattern of weather in a place over a long time.

history.etymology_note: English 'climate' came through Latin and Old French from Greek 'klima', meaning slope or inclination. It first referred to zones of the earth and later to the typical weather of a region.

senses.definition: A device that measures and shows the time.

history.etymology_note: From Middle Dutch clocke or Old French cloque, meaning bell. Early clocks announced the time by ringing bells rather than showing hands.

senses.definition: Awkward in movement or not skillful in action.

history.etymology_note: The word is related to Scandinavian forms suggesting heaviness or awkward mass. English uses it for unskillful or awkward movement and action.

senses.definition: Using force, pressure, or threats to make someone do something.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'coercere', meaning to restrain or control. English uses it for systems or acts that compel behavior through pressure rather than consent.

senses.definition: Clear, logical, and powerfully convincing.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'cogere', meaning to drive together or compel. English uses it for arguments that strongly compel belief because they are logical and clear.

senses.definition: To work jointly with others on a shared project or goal.

history.etymology_note: From Latin col- (together) + laborare (to work). The modern usage of creative joint work became widespread in the 19th century.

senses.definition: A small icy object in space that can form a glowing tail when near the sun.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'κομήτης' (kometes), meaning long-haired, through Latin forms. The name refers to the glowing tail that looks like streaming hair.

senses.definition: To help someone feel less sad, scared, or upset.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'conforter', based on Latin roots meaning to strengthen greatly. English uses it for giving emotional support and ease.

senses.definition: To look at two or more things to see how they are alike or different.

history.etymology_note: English 'compare' came through Old French from Latin 'comparare', meaning to match or liken. The word has long been used for judging similarity and difference.

senses.definition: A tool that shows direction, such as north, south, east, and west.

history.etymology_note: The word comes through Old French from Late Latin forms meaning to measure or pace out. In English, it became the name of the direction-finding instrument.

senses.definition: A feeling of caring deeply for someone who is suffering and wanting to help them.

history.etymology_note: From Latin compassio, meaning suffering together, from com- (together) + pati (to suffer). Entered English via Old French compassion.

senses.definition: Feeling concern for someone who is hurting and wanting to help.

history.etymology_note: Built through French and English from Late Latin 'compassio', meaning shared suffering. English uses it for sympathetic care joined with a wish to relieve pain.

senses.definition: To create or put together music, writing, or other art.

history.etymology_note: English 'compose' came through Old French from Latin 'componere', meaning to put together. The creative sense grew naturally from the idea of arranging parts into a whole.

senses.definition: A substance made from two or more different elements joined together chemically.

history.etymology_note: The scientific noun grew from the verb 'compound', which comes from Latin 'componere', meaning to put together. In chemistry, it refers to substances formed by combining elements.

senses.definition: Feeling sure that you can do something or handle it well.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'confidere', meaning to trust fully, through French forms. English uses it for trust in yourself or in how something will turn out.

senses.definition: Not understanding what is happening or what something means.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'confundere', meaning to pour together or mix up. English uses 'confused' for thoughts or situations that feel mixed up and unclear.

senses.definition: The inner sense that helps you know right from wrong.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'conscientia', meaning knowledge within oneself or moral awareness, through Old French forms. English uses it for the inward moral guide that judges actions.

senses.definition: Careful to think about how your actions affect other people.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'consider', from Latin 'considerare', meaning to examine carefully or reflect on. English uses the adjective for people who thoughtfully take others into account.

senses.definition: A named group of stars that forms a recognized pattern in the sky.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'constellatio', meaning a set of stars. English has long used it for star patterns recognized in astronomy and storytelling.

senses.definition: Feeling peaceful and satisfied with what you have or how things are.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'contentus', meaning satisfied or contained, through French forms. English uses it for a calm feeling of enoughness and satisfaction.

senses.definition: To work together with others toward a shared goal.

history.etymology_note: From Latin co- (together) + operari (to work), meaning to labor together. Entered English in the early 1600s.

senses.definition: A tall plant with yellow kernels growing on a cob, eaten as a vegetable.

history.etymology_note: From Old English corn, meaning grain in general. In American English it became specific to maize, while in British English it still means grain broadly.

senses.definition: The ability to face danger or fear with bravery.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'corage', meaning heart or bravery, ultimately derived from Latin 'cor', meaning heart.

senses.definition: Brave and willing to face fear or danger.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'courage', which came through Old French from Latin roots connected to the heart. English uses the adjective for brave action and bold spirit.

senses.definition: Polite, thoughtful, and showing good manners.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'courteis', meaning courtly or well-mann manners, from 'court'. English uses it for behavior marked by civility and consideration.

senses.definition: Polite and respectful behavior toward other people.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'courtoisie', meaning courtly manners, from 'court'. English uses it for good manners, respect, and civil behavior.

senses.definition: The child of your aunt or uncle.

history.etymology_note: English 'cousin' came through Old French 'cosin' from Latin 'consobrinus'. In older Latin, the word first referred more specifically to a cousin on the mother's side.

senses.definition: A sea creature with a hard shell, claws, and ten legs that walks sideways.

history.etymology_note: From Old English crabba, from Proto-Germanic *krabbô, related to the verb meaning to scratch or claw.

senses.definition: A bowl-shaped hole made by an eruption, explosion, or impact.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'κρατήρ' (krater), meaning a bowl or mixing vessel, through Latin forms. English applied the word to bowl-shaped hollows in the earth and on moons and planets.

senses.definition: The group of people who work together on a boat.

history.etymology_note: English 'crew' came through Old French forms meaning an increase or group. In English, it became a word for a company of sailors or workers together.

senses.definition: A circular ornament worn on the head by kings, queens, and royalty.
The top of the head, or the highest part of something like a tree or hill.

history.etymology_note: From Old French corone, from Latin corona meaning wreath or crown, which itself came from Greek korōnē (curved object).

senses.definition: Wanting to cause pain or not caring when others are hurt.

history.etymology_note: English 'cruel' came through Old French from Latin 'crudelis', meaning harsh or savage. It has long been used for people and actions that are painfully unkind.

senses.definition: The shared ways of life, ideas, arts, and traditions of a group of people.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'cultura', which first meant cultivation or tending the land. In English, the meaning expanded from growing and training to the broader shared life of a community.

senses.definition: A strong desire to learn or know more about something.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'curiositas', meaning careful inquiry or eagerness to know, entering English through scholarly and philosophical writing.

senses.definition: Wanting to know more about something.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'curiosus', meaning careful, eager to know, or inquisitive. English kept the sense of wanting to learn more.

senses.definition: A steady movement of water or air in one direction.

history.etymology_note: The word comes through Old French forms from Latin 'currere', meaning to run. English uses it for flowing motion in water, air, and later electricity.

senses.definition: The first light of day in the morning.

history.etymology_note: English 'dawn' developed from Middle English forms related to Old English 'dagung' and the verb 'dagian', meaning to become day. The word has kept its core meaning of daybreak.

senses.definition: Trying to mislead people by hiding the truth or lying.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'deceit', which came through Old French from Latin roots meaning to ensnare or mislead, plus the suffix '-ful'. The adjective means full of deceit or dishonesty.

senses.definition: The quality of behaving in a fair, honest, and proper way toward others.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'decent', from Latin 'decens', meaning fitting or proper. English uses 'decency' for basic moral goodness and proper conduct.

senses.definition: To give all your time and effort to something important to you.

history.etymology_note: From Latin dedicare, meaning to devote or set apart for a purpose, from de- (away) + dicare (to proclaim or consecrate).

senses.definition: Going far down from the top or surface.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'dēop', meaning deep or profound. It is an inherited Germanic word used for physical depth and later for ideas and feelings.

senses.definition: Respectful willingness to yield to another person's judgment or wishes.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'deferre', meaning to carry down or yield, through French forms. English uses it for respectful submission or regard toward another person.

senses.definition: Able to be trusted to do what is needed.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'depend', from Latin 'dependere', meaning to hang from or rely on. The adjective means fit to be relied on.

senses.definition: Firmly decided to keep trying until a goal is reached.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'determinare', meaning to set limits or decide, through French and English development. The adjective came to mean fixed in purpose and hard to turn aside.

senses.definition: Deeply committed and full of steady care or love.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'devotus', meaning vowed or dedicated, from 'devovere', to vow or dedicate. English uses it for strong commitment, loyalty, and loving care.

senses.definition: A form of a language that is spoken in a certain place or by a certain group of people.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'διάλεκτος' (dialektos), meaning conversation or way of speaking. In English, it came to mean a regional or social variety of a language.

senses.definition: Intended to teach, sometimes in a way that feels too obvious or moralizing.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'διδακτικός' (didaktikos), meaning apt at teaching, from 'didaskein', to teach. English uses it both neutrally and critically for teaching-oriented language or art.

senses.definition: Modest and lacking confidence in speaking or acting.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'diffidere', meaning to distrust or lack confidence. In English, it came to describe shy self-doubt or modest reserve.

senses.definition: Careful and steady in doing work or trying to reach a goal.

history.etymology_note: English 'diligent' came through Old French from Latin 'diligens', meaning attentive or careful. The word has long described steady, serious effort.

senses.definition: Feeling sad because something did not happen the way you hoped.

history.etymology_note: English 'disappoint' came through French from roots meaning to remove from an appointed hope or expectation. The adjective describes the feeling when hopes are not met.

senses.definition: Able to notice subtle differences and judge quality well.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'discernere', meaning to separate or distinguish. In English, it came to describe refined perception and careful judgment.

senses.definition: The practice of training yourself to follow rules and build good habits.

history.etymology_note: From Latin disciplina, meaning instruction or training, from discipulus (a learner). Related to discere (to learn).

senses.definition: Moving from topic to topic without staying tightly focused.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'discursus', meaning running about, from 'discurrere', to run in different directions. English uses it for speech or writing that ranges broadly rather than staying narrow.

senses.definition: Feeling a strong dislike because something seems gross or wrong.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'disgust', which came through French and Latin roots tied to taste. English uses it for strong dislike, especially when something feels gross or offensive.

senses.definition: Showing that you do not think something or someone is worth serious attention.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'dismiss', from Latin 'dimittere', meaning to send away. English uses the adjective for attitudes that brush something aside as unimportant.

senses.definition: Calm and impartial because emotion is kept out of judgment.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from 'passion', from Latin 'passio', with the negative prefix 'dis-'. It came to mean free from emotional bias or intense feeling.

senses.definition: A place beside the water where boats can stop and be tied up.

history.etymology_note: English 'dock' was borrowed from Dutch or Middle Dutch. It has long been used for a place where ships are kept, repaired, or tied up.

senses.definition: A furry four-legged animal kept as a pet, known for loyalty and barking.

history.etymology_note: From Old English docga, a rare word that surpassed the previous standard term 'hund' by the 16th century. Its ultimate origin is unknown.

senses.definition: Showing stubborn and determined persistence.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from 'dog', from the idea of following or holding on like a dog. The adjective came to mean persistent in a stubborn, determined way.

senses.definition: A highly intelligent ocean mammal that swims in groups and communicates with clicks and whistles.

history.etymology_note: From Greek delphis, possibly related to delphys (womb), referring to the dolphin's mammal nature. Entered English via Old French dauphin and Latin delphinus.

senses.definition: A large mythical creature with wings, claws, and the ability to breathe fire.

history.etymology_note: From Old French dragon, from Latin draco, from Greek drakon meaning serpent or dragon. The word is related to a root meaning to watch or see sharply, like a creature with piercing eyes.

senses.definition: To move a ball forward in sports by tapping or bouncing it while running.

history.etymology_note: From Middle English 'dribben', meaning to fall in drops, later extended to sports where a ball moves forward in small repeated motions.

senses.definition: To move slowly as if carried by water, wind, or another force.

history.etymology_note: English 'drift' is related to Old Norse 'drifa', meaning to drive or move along. It came to describe slow carried motion in water, air, or snow.

senses.definition: Strongly motivated to work hard and reach a goal.

history.etymology_note: Built from the verb 'drive', from Old English 'drīfan', meaning to force, push, or urge forward. The adjective developed the figurative sense of being strongly pushed by purpose.

senses.definition: A percussion instrument played by striking a membrane stretched over a hollow frame.

history.etymology_note: From Middle Dutch tromme or trom, meaning drum. Possibly of imitative origin, based on the sound the instrument makes.

senses.definition: A water bird with a flat beak and webbed feet that can swim and quack.

history.etymology_note: From Old English dūce, believed to come from the verb 'duck' (to dive), reflecting the bird's diving behavior.

senses.definition: The darker time in the evening just after the sun goes down.

history.etymology_note: The word likely comes from Middle English forms related to Old English 'dox', meaning dark or swarthy. In English, it came to name the dim evening light before night.

senses.definition: Something you are supposed to do because it is right or expected.

history.etymology_note: English 'duty' came through Anglo-French from forms meaning what is owed or due. It developed into the important sense of obligation and responsibility.

senses.definition: To live in a place.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'dwellan', which earlier could mean to lead astray or delay, but later developed the meaning of remaining or staying in a place. Modern English keeps the residence sense.

senses.definition: A large, powerful bird of prey with sharp talons and excellent eyesight.

history.etymology_note: From Old French aigle, from Latin aquila. Replaced the Old English term earn in Middle English. Used as a symbol of power in many nations.

senses.definition: Serious and sincere in purpose, feeling, or effort.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'eornoste', meaning zeal, seriousness, or vigor. English kept the sense of heartfelt seriousness and sincere effort.

senses.definition: A sound that is heard again after it bounces off a surface.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἠχώ' (echo), meaning reflected sound, through Latin forms. The word was also the name of a figure in Greek mythology linked to repeated sound.

senses.definition: A community of all living things and their environment working together.

history.etymology_note: A modern scientific term coined in 1935, from Greek oikos (house or environment) + system. Created by botanist Arthur Tansley to describe ecological communities.

senses.definition: An oval object laid by birds, reptiles, and fish that contains a developing baby animal.

history.etymology_note: From Old Norse egg, it replaced the Old English æg. The word is related to Latin ovum, from which we get oval and ovary.

senses.definition: A basic chemical substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'elementum', meaning first principle or basic part. In English science, it became the name for the simplest chemical substances such as oxygen or gold.

senses.definition: The largest land animal, with thick gray skin, big ears, and a long trunk.

history.etymology_note: From Greek elephas, meaning elephant or ivory, entering English through Latin elephantus and Old French olifant. The ivory connection links the animal to its tusks.

senses.definition: Expressing ideas clearly, beautifully, and persuasively.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'eloquens', meaning speaking out or speaking well, from 'eloqui', to speak out. English uses it for language that is both graceful and persuasive.

senses.definition: Difficult to find, catch, define, or fully understand.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'eludere', meaning to escape from or mock by slipping away. English uses it for things that avoid clear capture, whether physical or intellectual.

senses.definition: Feeling uncomfortable because you think other people noticed a mistake or awkward moment.

history.etymology_note: From French 'embarrasser', meaning to block, tangle, or hinder. English developed the emotional sense of feeling socially awkward or self-conscious.

senses.definition: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person.

history.etymology_note: From Greek empatheia meaning physical affection or passion, from em- (in) + pathos (feeling). Adopted into English psychology in the 1900s.

senses.definition: The ability to keep going and stay strong during a long or difficult activity.

history.etymology_note: From Old French endurance, from endurer (to endure), ultimately from Latin indurare (to harden). Associated with athletic stamina since the 18th century.

senses.definition: Bold energy and willingness to take action on difficult plans or goals.

history.etymology_note: From Old French forms based on 'entreprendre', meaning to undertake. English uses it for bold undertaking, initiative, and energetic action.

senses.definition: Wanting something good that belongs to someone else.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'envy', which came through French from Latin 'invidia', meaning envy or ill will. English uses 'envious' for the feeling of wanting what someone else has.

senses.definition: Lasting for only a very short time.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἐφήμερος' (ephemeros), meaning lasting only a day. English uses it more broadly for anything brief, fleeting, or short-lived.

senses.definition: Mental calmness and balance, especially in a difficult situation.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'aequanimitas', meaning evenness of mind. English kept the sense of steady emotional balance under pressure.

senses.definition: Open to more than one meaning and not clearly decided or stated.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'aequivocus', meaning having the same name or ambiguous. English uses it for words, statements, or attitudes that are unclear or uncertain.

senses.definition: The wearing away of rock or soil by water, wind, ice, or other natural forces.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'erodere', meaning to gnaw away, through French and Latin forms. In earth science, English uses it for the gradual wearing down of land and rock.

senses.definition: Having deep learning and wide knowledge from serious study.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'eruditus', meaning instructed or educated. English uses it for highly learned people, especially in intellectual or literary contexts.

senses.definition: Intended for or understood by only a small, specialized group.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἐσωτερικός' (esoterikos), meaning inner or belonging to an inner circle. English uses it for knowledge or interests limited to a small group of initiates or experts.

senses.definition: To make a close guess based on what you know.

history.etymology_note: English 'estimate' comes through French and Latin from 'aestimare', meaning to value or assess. In modern use, it often means making a reasoned approximation.

senses.definition: Following accepted ideas of right and wrong.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἠθικός' (ethikos), meaning relating to character or moral custom, through Latin forms. English uses it for behavior guided by moral standards.

senses.definition: A shared identity based on culture, ancestry, language, or traditions.

history.etymology_note: The English word was formed from 'ethnic', which comes from Greek 'ἔθνος' (ethnos), meaning nation or people. 'Ethnicity' became common in modern social science for cultural or ancestral identity.

senses.definition: The study of where a word comes from and how its form and meaning changed over time.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἐτυμολογία' (etymologia), meaning the study of the true sense of a word, through Latin and Old French forms. In English, it became the term for tracing word origins and development.

senses.definition: To judge the quality, value, or meaning of something carefully.

history.etymology_note: English borrowed the verb from French 'évaluer', meaning to determine value. The word is used broadly in English for careful judgment, not just money value.

senses.definition: Facts or signs that help show whether something is true.

history.etymology_note: English 'evidence' came through Old French from Late Latin 'evidentia'. It first referred to visible or clear appearance and later to proof or grounds for belief.

senses.definition: Bringing strong images, memories, or feelings to mind.

history.etymology_note: Built from Latin 'evocare', meaning to call out or summon. English uses it for words, images, or sounds that summon vivid mental or emotional responses.

senses.definition: To change gradually over time, becoming more complex or developed.

history.etymology_note: From Latin evolvere, meaning to unroll or unfold, from e- (out) + volvere (to roll). Applied to biological change after Darwin published his theory in 1859.

senses.definition: Feeling happy and full of energy because something good is happening or about to happen.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'excitare', meaning to call out, stir up, or awaken. English uses 'excited' for strong stirred-up feelings and energy.

senses.definition: Clearly and directly stated without leaving doubt.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'explicitus', meaning unfolded or set forth, from 'explicare', to unfold. English uses it for meanings that are clearly expressed and fully stated.

senses.definition: Treating people in an equal and right way.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'fæger', which first meant pleasing, beautiful, or favorable. English later developed the strong moral sense of just and impartial.

senses.definition: Very concerned with accuracy, cleanliness, taste, or detail.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'fastidiosus', meaning disdainful, squeamish, or hard to please. English uses it for people with exacting standards in detail, order, or taste.

senses.definition: The feeling that something dangerous or bad may happen.

history.etymology_note: Old English 'fǣr' first meant sudden danger or calamity. English later developed the strong emotional sense of fear as the feeling of danger.

senses.definition: The emotions inside you, such as happy, sad, scared, or excited.

history.etymology_note: Built from the English verb 'feel', from Old English 'fēlan', plus the noun ending '-ing'. English uses it for both bodily sensations and emotions.

senses.definition: The light, heat, and flame produced when something is burning.

history.etymology_note: From Old English fȳr, from Proto-Germanic *fūr. Related to Greek pyr and Latin focus (hearth), from which we get focus and fuel.

senses.definition: A cold-blooded animal with scales and fins that lives in water and breathes through gills.

history.etymology_note: From Old English fisc, one of the oldest words in English, related to Latin piscis (from which we get Pisces) and Greek ikhthýs.

senses.definition: A piece of cloth with colors or patterns that represents a country, team, or group.

history.etymology_note: The English word flag appeared in the 1500s, possibly adapted from Dutch vlag. Its ultimate origin is unclear.

senses.definition: To stay on top of water without sinking.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'flotian', meaning to float or drift on water. The word has kept that same central meaning.

senses.definition: The colorful part of a plant that blooms and often has a pleasant smell.

history.etymology_note: From Old French flor, from Latin flos (stem flor-), meaning blossom. Related to flora, the term for plant life.

senses.definition: A young horse.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'fola', meaning foal. The word is inherited from Germanic and stayed a standard term for a young horse.

senses.definition: Patient self-control and restraint, especially when provoked.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from the verb 'forbear', from Old English 'forberan', meaning to bear with, abstain, or endure. The noun came to mean patient restraint and tolerance.

senses.definition: A prediction about what the weather or future events will be like.

history.etymology_note: Formed from Old English 'fore' meaning before and later English 'cast', combining to describe predicting something ahead of time.

senses.definition: Willing to stop feeling angry after someone does something wrong.

history.etymology_note: Built from the verb 'forgive', from Old English 'forgiefan', meaning to give up a claim or pardon. The adjective describes a person ready to pardon rather than hold resentment.

senses.definition: Causing respect or fear because of great strength, skill, or difficulty.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'formidare', meaning to fear, through French forms. English uses it for people, tasks, or forces impressive enough to inspire respect or fear.

senses.definition: Strength of mind that helps someone face pain, fear, or hardship bravely.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'fortitudo', meaning strength or bravery, from 'fortis', strong. It has long been used in moral and philosophical writing for courage in adversity.

senses.definition: A number that names part of a whole.

history.etymology_note: From Anglo-French and Late Latin forms based on Latin 'fractio', meaning a breaking. That history matches the modern idea of a whole being broken into parts.

senses.definition: Easy to break, damage, or hurt.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'fragilis', meaning breakable, through French forms. English uses it for delicate objects and sometimes for living living things or conditions.

senses.definition: A small amphibian with smooth skin, strong back legs for jumping, and webbed feet for swimming.

history.etymology_note: From Old English frogga, a common word in the Germanic languages. Its ultimate origin is unknown, though it is thought to be onomatopoeic.

senses.definition: A thin layer of ice that forms when the air is very cold.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'forst', later also 'frost', meaning freezing cold or frozen moisture. The word is inherited from early Germanic and has stayed close to that meaning.

senses.definition: Feeling upset because something is hard, blocked, or not going the way you want.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'frustrari', meaning to disappoint or make useless. English uses 'frustrated' for the feeling of being blocked from success.

senses.definition: A huge system of stars, gas, and dust held together in space.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'γαλαξίας' (galaxias), meaning milky, from 'gala' meaning milk. The word first referred to the Milky Way and later to vast star systems in general.

senses.definition: A piece of ground where flowers, fruits, or vegetables are grown.

history.etymology_note: English 'garden' came from Old North French 'gardin'. That form is tied to older Germanic words meaning an enclosed place, which fits the idea of a fenced growing area.

senses.definition: Talking a great deal, often more than is necessary.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'garrulus', meaning talkative or chattering. English often uses it for speech that is excessive or rambling.

senses.definition: A state of matter that spreads out to fill the space around it.

history.etymology_note: The scientific word was introduced in Dutch by Jan Baptista van Helmont, probably influenced by Greek 'chaos'. English borrowed it for substances like air that do not keep a fixed shape or volume.

senses.definition: To bring things or people together into one place.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'gadrian', meaning to collect or unite. It is an old Germanic action word used in both daily life and farming.

senses.definition: Willing to give, share, or help more than is required.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'generosus', which first meant noble or of good birth. English later developed the strong sense of freely giving and noble-hearted kindness.

senses.definition: Warm, cheerful, and pleasantly friendly.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'genialis', meaning festive, pleasant, or related to marriage and household spirit. English developed the sense of kindly warmth and cheer.

senses.definition: Soft, calm, and careful in the way you act or touch.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'gentil', which first meant noble or well-born, from Latin 'gentilis'. In English, the word shifted toward the common meaning of mild, kind, and soft in manner.

senses.definition: The study of the earth's places, land, water, and the people who live there.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'γεωγραφία' (geographia), literally meaning earth-description. English uses it for the study of places, environments, and spatial relationships.

senses.definition: The spirit of a dead person, imagined as an invisible or see-through presence.

history.etymology_note: From Old English gāst, meaning spirit or soul. The h was added in the 15th century under Flemish printing influence. Originally referred to the soul, not a haunting spirit.

senses.definition: The tallest animal on Earth, with a very long neck and spotted coat, native to Africa.

history.etymology_note: From Arabic zarāfa, possibly from an African language meaning fast-walker. Entered English through Italian giraffa and French girafe.

senses.definition: A large, slow-moving mass of ice formed over many years.

history.etymology_note: English borrowed the word from French 'glacier', based on French and Latin words for ice. It became the standard scientific and geographic term for large ice masses.

senses.definition: To shine with a faint or wavering light.

history.etymology_note: From Middle English 'glimeren', related to older Germanic words for shining dimly. The word has long described a soft or flickering light.

senses.definition: A point scored by sending a ball into a designated area; or an object of a person's ambition.

history.etymology_note: Originally meaning a boundary or limit; potentially from Old English 'gal' (obstacle).

senses.definition: The system or group of people that makes rules and decisions for a country, state, or city.

history.etymology_note: English borrowed the word from Old French 'governement', from the verb meaning to govern or steer. That verb traces back to Greek and Latin roots meaning to guide or direct.

senses.definition: Moving or acting in a smooth, pleasing, and controlled way.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'grace', from Latin 'gratia', meaning favor, thanks, or elegance, plus the suffix '-ful'. English uses it for pleasing ease in motion or manner.

senses.definition: Kind, warm, and pleasant in the way you treat others.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'gratiosus', meaning pleasing, favorable, or full of grace, through Old French forms. English uses it for kindness, elegance, and generous courtesy.

senses.definition: The rules for how words are used together in a language.

history.etymology_note: English 'grammar' came through Latin and Old French from Greek 'grammatike', meaning the art of letters. In English, the meaning narrowed to the rules and structure of language.

senses.definition: To take hold of something firmly with the hand.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'grǣpsian', meaning to seize or clutch. The word remains a strong everyday verb for holding tightly.

senses.definition: Feeling thankful for kindness, help, or good things.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'grate', an older form related to favor and thanks, ultimately from Latin 'gratus', pleasing or thankful. English uses it for warm thankfulness and appreciation.

senses.definition: Dignity, seriousness, and weight of manner or character.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'gravitas', meaning weight or seriousness. Although related forms existed earlier, the current English high-register use became especially prominent in modern public and political language.

senses.definition: The invisible force that pulls objects toward the earth.

history.etymology_note: From Latin gravitas, meaning weight or seriousness, from gravis (heavy). Popularized in physics by Isaac Newton in the late 1600s.

senses.definition: Wanting too much for yourself and not wanting to share.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'grǣdig', meaning hungry, eager, or greedy. English kept the sense of wanting more than is right or fair.

senses.definition: Very serious, harsh, or unpleasant.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'grim', meaning fierce, cruel, or severe. It is an old inherited Germanic adjective that stayed close to its earlier meaning.

senses.definition: Courage and determination to keep going even when something is hard.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'grēot', meaning small stones or coarse sand. English later used it figuratively for hard toughness of spirit.

senses.definition: A small group of trees growing close together.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'grāf', meaning a grove or small wood. It is an old inherited Germanic word for clustered trees.

senses.definition: Feeling a little cross, cranky, or hard to please.

history.etymology_note: Built from English 'grump', a word for complaining or ill temper. English uses 'grumpy' for mild bad mood or irritability.

senses.definition: Sincere, innocent, and free from trickery or deceit.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from 'guile', a word of Scandinavian origin related to trickery, plus the suffix '-less'. The adjective means lacking deceit or cunning.

senses.definition: A musical instrument with a long neck and strings that are plucked or strummed.

history.etymology_note: From Spanish guitarra, which came from Arabic qītār, itself from Greek kithara (a lyre-like instrument). The modern guitar form developed in Spain.

senses.definition: The natural environment where an animal or plant normally lives and grows.

history.etymology_note: From Latin habitare, meaning to dwell or inhabit, from habere (to have or hold). First used in natural history texts in the 1700s.

senses.definition: A tool with a heavy metal head used to drive nails into wood or break things apart.

history.etymology_note: From Old English hamor, from Proto-Germanic *hamaraz. Related to Norse hamarr, meaning stone cliff, reflecting early stone hammer tools.

senses.definition: Feeling good, glad, or full of joy.

history.etymology_note: English 'happy' is related to Old Norse 'happ', meaning luck or chance. It first suggested good fortune and later came to mean feeling pleased or glad.

senses.definition: A sheltered place where boats can stay safely near the shore.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'herebeorg', originally meaning shelter or lodging. In time, English specialized the word for safe places where ships could stay.

senses.definition: A pleasing combination of musical notes played or sung together.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'harmonia', meaning joining or fitting together, later used in music theory to describe pleasing combinations of tones.

senses.definition: The time when crops are gathered from the field, or the crops that are gathered.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'hærfest', which once meant the autumn season as well as gathering crops. Over time, English kept the farming sense while 'autumn' became the common season word.

senses.definition: A very strong feeling of dislike.

history.etymology_note: Built from Old English 'hatian', meaning to hate. English has long used it for intense dislike.

senses.definition: The organ in your chest that pumps blood through your body; also a symbol of love.

history.etymology_note: From Old English heorte, from Proto-Germanic *hertô. One of the oldest words in English, with roots going back to Proto-Indo-European *kerd.

senses.definition: The floor or area in front of a fireplace, or the home as a warm gathering place.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'heorð', meaning hearth or fireplace. The word has long carried both the literal meaning of a fire place and the wider sense of home.

senses.definition: A low plant with many small purple or pink flowers that grows on open land.

history.etymology_note: The word comes from Old English plant-name forms related to 'hǣddre'. English kept it as the common name for this hardy flowering plant of moors and heaths.

senses.definition: The wheel or handle used to steer a boat.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'helma', meaning rudder or steering gear. In modern English, it came to mean the steering position or steering device of a ship.

senses.definition: A hard protective covering worn on the head for safety in sports or battle.

history.etymology_note: From Old French helme, a diminutive of helme (helmet), from Old High German helm (protection). Related to the English word helm.

senses.definition: Ready and willing to give help.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from 'help', from Old English 'helpan', plus the suffix '-ful'. It means full of help or inclined to help.

senses.definition: To pause because you are unsure or nervous about what to do.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'haesitare', meaning to stick fast or be uncertain. English uses it for a pause caused by doubt or uncertainty.

senses.definition: The study of people, places, and events from the past.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'ἱστορία' (historia), meaning inquiry or knowledge gained by investigation, through Latin and French forms. In English, it came to refer to accounts and study of the past.

senses.definition: Telling the truth and not trying to trick or lie to others.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'honestus', meaning honorable or respected, entering English through Old French as a term describing moral integrity.

senses.definition: A strong sense of what is right, fair, and worthy of respect.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'honor', meaning esteem, dignity, or public respect, through Old French forms. English uses it for both earned respect and principled conduct.

senses.definition: Deserving respect because of honesty, fairness, and strong principles.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'honorabilis', meaning worthy of honor, through Old French forms. English uses it for people and actions that merit high respect.

senses.definition: The feeling that something good may happen.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'hopa', meaning expectation or confidence for the future. English has long used it for positive expectation.

senses.definition: Feeling that something good may happen.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'hope', from Old English 'hopa', plus the suffix '-ful'. English uses it for a feeling of expectation for good things.

senses.definition: A large strong animal with hooves and a mane, used for riding and pulling.

history.etymology_note: From Old English hors, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą. Related to Old Norse hross and Old High German hros.

senses.definition: A building where people live, with rooms for sleeping, cooking, and relaxing.

history.etymology_note: From Old English hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsan. It originally referred simply to a shelter or dwelling place.

senses.definition: The main body of a boat that floats on the water.

history.etymology_note: The word is related to Old English 'hulu', meaning a husk or outer covering. In English, it came to mean the outer body of a ship.

senses.definition: Not thinking of yourself as better than others; modest about your abilities.

history.etymology_note: From Latin humilis, meaning low or grounded, from humus (earth or ground). The idea of being close to the earth became associated with modesty.

senses.definition: The quality of being modest and not acting as if you are better than others.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'humilitas', meaning lowliness or modesty, from 'humilis', low. English uses it for modest self-understanding rather than arrogance.

senses.definition: Feeling pain in your body or sadness in your heart.

history.etymology_note: English 'hurt' came through Old French from a verb meaning to strike or collide. English broadened it to include both physical pain and emotional pain.

senses.definition: The process of drinking enough water to keep your body healthy and working properly.

history.etymology_note: Formed from Greek hydor (water) + the suffix -ation. First used in chemistry before becoming common in health and sports science.

senses.definition: Arrogantly commanding and expecting immediate obedience.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'imperiosus', meaning commanding or mighty, from 'imperium', command or authority. English uses it for overbearing dominance in manner or speech.

senses.definition: Not easily upset, disturbed, or thrown off balance.

history.etymology_note: Built from Latin roots meaning to disturb or confuse, with the negative prefix 'im-'. English uses it for remarkable calmness under stress.

senses.definition: Acting quickly and forcefully without enough thought.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'impetuosus', meaning violent or rushing, from 'impetus'. English uses it for behavior driven by sudden force or impulse.

senses.definition: Not yet fully formed, organized, or clearly developed.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'incohatus', meaning begun or just started, from 'inchoare', to begin. English uses it for early, incomplete, or not-yet-shaped ideas and conditions.

senses.definition: Sharp, clear, and quick in thought or expression.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'incisus', meaning cut into, from the verb 'incidere'. English uses it figuratively for speech or thought that cuts sharply to the point.

senses.definition: Not thinking about how your actions affect other people.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'considerate' with the negative prefix 'in-'. It means lacking thoughtful regard for others.

senses.definition: Never seeming to grow tired in effort or energy.

history.etymology_note: Built from Latin roots meaning to tire out, with the negative prefix 'in-'. English uses it for tireless persistence.

senses.definition: Working hard and staying busy in a useful way.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'industria', meaning diligence, purpose, or activity, through French forms. English uses it for steady, productive hard work.

senses.definition: Impossible to stop, persuade, or prevent.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'inexorabilis', meaning not to be moved by entreaty, from 'exorare', to persuade by pleading. English uses it for relentless forces, processes, or outcomes.

senses.definition: To figure out something from clues instead of being told directly.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'inferre', meaning to bring in or bring to. In English, it developed the sense of drawing a conclusion from what is known.

senses.definition: The habit of acting and getting started without waiting to be told.

history.etymology_note: Built from French and Latin roots based on 'initium', meaning beginning. English uses it for the power or readiness to begin action independently.

senses.definition: To introduce new ideas or methods that change the way something is done.

history.etymology_note: From Latin innovare, meaning to renew or alter, from in- (into) + novus (new). Entered English to describe bringing in new ideas or methods.

senses.definition: The quality of being honest, whole, and doing what is right even when no one is watching.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'integritas', meaning wholeness, soundness, or uprightness, from 'integer', whole or untouched. English uses it for moral honesty and for the state of being complete and unbroken.

senses.definition: To explain the meaning of something or understand what it means.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'interpretari', meaning to explain or translate. English kept both ideas of understanding meaning and explaining it to others.

senses.definition: Fearless and ready to face danger or uncertainty.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'intrepidus', meaning unalarmed or fearless. English uses it for bold courage in risky or uncertain situations.

senses.definition: Quick to understand something without needing every step explained.

history.etymology_note: From Late Latin 'intuitivus', from Latin 'intueri', meaning to look at closely or consider. English uses it for direct understanding that feels immediate rather than step-by-step.

senses.definition: To create something new that did not exist before.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'invenire', meaning to come upon or discover, entering English to describe creating or designing new things.

senses.definition: To look closely into something in order to find facts or answers.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'investigare', meaning to track out or search into. English has long used it for careful inquiry and fact-finding.

senses.definition: Feeling upset because you want what someone else has or gets.

history.etymology_note: English 'jealous' came through Old French from Latin and Greek roots tied to strong feeling and rivalry. English uses it for envy and fear of losing attention or love.

senses.definition: A trip from one place to another.

history.etymology_note: English 'journey' came from Old French 'journée', which originally meant a day's time, travel, or work. It is related to Latin words for 'day', showing how the idea began as a day's travel.

senses.definition: A strong feeling of happiness and delight.

history.etymology_note: English 'joy' came through Old French from Latin 'gaudia', meaning rejoicing or delight. It has long meant deep happiness.

senses.definition: Showing careful thought and good sense in making decisions.

history.etymology_note: Built on Latin 'judicium', meaning judgment or decision, through French and English development. It came to mean showing sound judgment rather than merely relating to judges.

senses.definition: Morally right and guided by fairness.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'justus', meaning lawful, righteous, or fair, through Old French forms. English uses it for justice, fairness, and moral rightness.

senses.definition: To give good reasons for why something is right, fair, or true.

history.etymology_note: English borrowed the word from Old French 'justifier', based on Latin roots meaning to make just. The modern sense centers on giving reasons or showing fairness.

senses.definition: A large marsupial from Australia that hops on its powerful back legs and carries its young in a pouch.

history.etymology_note: From Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal Australian language. Recorded by Captain Cook's expedition in 1770 — a rare example of an English word sourced directly from an Indigenous Australian language.

senses.definition: A small metal device used to open a lock.

history.etymology_note: From Old English cæg, meaning key, of unknown ultimate origin. One of the few English words with no clear relatives in other Germanic languages.

senses.definition: To strike or propel something forcibly with the foot.

history.etymology_note: Possibly of Scandinavian origin, replacing the Old English 'fyllan' (to strike).

senses.definition: People who are related to you by family.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'cynn', meaning family, race, or kind. It is one of the oldest English words for family connection and shared descent.

senses.definition: The habit of being gentle, helpful, and good to other people.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from 'kind' and the suffix '-ness'. Older English forms connected 'kind' with natural feeling and family relation, and the word later developed the sense of warm, good-hearted behavior.

senses.definition: A light frame covered with cloth or paper, flown in the wind on a string.

history.etymology_note: From Old English cȳta, originally referring to the kite bird. The flying toy was named after the hovering bird in the 17th century.

senses.definition: A tool with a sharp blade used for cutting food or other materials.

history.etymology_note: From Old Norse knífr, a word adopted into Old English. The initial k was originally pronounced but became silent in the 17th century.

senses.definition: What a person knows from learning, study, or experience.

history.etymology_note: From Old English forms built from the verb meaning 'to know'. The word has long meant understanding gained through awareness, study, or experience.

senses.definition: Using very few words in a clear and direct way.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'Λακωνικός' (Lakonikos), meaning from Laconia, the region of Sparta. The Spartans were famous for brief speech, leading English to use the word for concise expression.

senses.definition: A frame of two long poles joined by steps, used for climbing up or down.

history.etymology_note: From Old English hlæder, from Proto-Germanic *hlaidri. Related to the verb lean, as ladders lean against walls.

senses.definition: A device that produces light, either by burning oil or using electricity.

history.etymology_note: From Old French lampe, from Latin lampas, from Greek lampas (torch or light), from lampein (to shine).

senses.definition: A system of words and rules that people use to speak, write, and share ideas.

history.etymology_note: English borrowed the word from Old French 'langage', based on Latin 'lingua', meaning tongue or language. The word has long referred both to speech in general and to specific systems like English or Spanish.

senses.definition: A lamp with a cover around it that protects the light.

history.etymology_note: English 'lantern' came through Old French from Latin 'lanterna', meaning a lamp or torch. The word has long referred to a protected portable light.

senses.definition: Present but hidden or not yet active.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'latens', meaning lying hidden, from 'latere', to be hidden. English uses it for qualities, powers, or conditions that exist without being visible or active.

senses.definition: To make happy sounds when something feels funny or joyful.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'hliehhan', meaning to laugh. It is one of the oldest English words for this joyful action.

senses.definition: The flat green part of a plant that grows from a stem or branch.
A single page of a book, including the front and back together.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'lēaf', meaning leaf of a plant or tree, a term that has remained largely unchanged in modern English.

senses.definition: Feeling sad because other people did not include you.

history.etymology_note: This is an English phrase built from common words meaning not included or omitted. It became a common way to describe the feeling of exclusion.

senses.definition: The set of words used in a language or by a person, group, or subject.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'λεξικόν' (lexikon), meaning a book of words. In English, it came to mean both a dictionary and the word-stock of a language or field.

senses.definition: A place where many books are kept so people can read or borrow them.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'librarium', meaning a place for books, entering English through Old French as a term for collections of written works.

senses.definition: A large wild cat with a mane that lives in Africa and is known as the king of the jungle.

history.etymology_note: From Old French lion, from Latin leo, from Greek leōn. A symbol of courage and royalty in many ancient cultures.

senses.definition: A state of matter that can flow and take the shape of its container.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'liquidus', meaning flowing or clear, through French and Latin forms. In English science, it became the name of the flowing state of matter.

senses.definition: Written works such as stories, poems, and plays that people read and study.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'litteratura', meaning writing formed from letters. In English, it came to mean written works, especially those valued for thought or art.

senses.definition: A way of thinking that uses clear steps and reasons to reach a correct answer.

history.etymology_note: Derived from Greek 'logikos', meaning related to reason or speech, and adopted in medieval scholarship to describe structured reasoning.

senses.definition: The feeling of being sad because you feel alone or not included.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from 'lonely' plus the noun ending '-ness'. It names the feeling of being emotionally alone.

senses.definition: Feeling sad because you want company or connection.

history.etymology_note: Built in English from ideas related to being alone, with the adjective ending '-ly'. English uses it for the feeling of sadness from lacking companionship.

senses.definition: Very talkative and likely to speak at length.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'loquax', meaning talkative, from 'loqui', to speak. English uses it for unusually free or abundant speech.

senses.definition: A strong feeling of care and affection for someone or something.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'lufu', meaning love or deep affection. It is one of the oldest core English emotion words.

senses.definition: Faithful and steady in support of a person, team, cause, or promise.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'loial', meaning lawful or faithful, ultimately from Latin 'legalis', relating to law. English kept the idea of faithfulness and dependable allegiance.

senses.definition: Clear, easy to understand, and free from confusion.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'lucidus', meaning bright or clear. English extended the idea of brightness to clarity of language and thought.

senses.definition: Feeling angry or upset.

history.etymology_note: Old English forms related to 'mad' first meant out of one's mind or foolish. In modern everyday English, especially American English, it commonly means angry.

senses.definition: Showing a noble spirit and being generous or forgiving toward a rival or less powerful person.

history.etymology_note: From 'magnus' (great) + 'animus' (mind/soul). Literally translated as being 'big-minded'.

senses.definition: Having or showing a wish to harm others.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'malevolens', meaning ill-disposed or wishing evil, from 'male', badly, and 'velle', to wish. English uses it for harmful ill will.

senses.definition: Harmful, dangerous, or driven by ill will.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'malignus', meaning evil-disposed or harmful. English uses it for both moral hostility and harmful medical or social conditions.

senses.definition: A drawing or picture that shows where places are in an area or the world.

history.etymology_note: From Medieval Latin mappa mundi (map of the world), where mappa originally meant cloth or napkin — early maps were drawn on cloth.

senses.definition: Related to the sea or ocean.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'marinus', meaning of the sea, through French forms. English uses it for sea life, sea environments, and things connected with the ocean.

senses.definition: A tall pole on a boat that holds up the sails.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'mæst', meaning the mast of a ship. The word has kept the same core nautical meaning in English for many centuries.
