history.etymology_note: From Latin 'differentia' (distance/distinction). Subtraction finds the numerical 'difference' or distance between two values.

senses.definition: The symbol that shows two amounts or expressions are equal.

history.etymology_note: Invented by Robert Recorde in 1557 because 'no two things can be more equal' than two parallel lines of the same length.

senses.definition: The symbol that shows one value is larger than another.

history.etymology_note: A comparative compound. The symbol (>) opens its wide side toward the larger number to show its greater magnitude.

senses.definition: The symbol that shows one value is smaller than another.

history.etymology_note: A comparative compound. The symbol (<) points its small, sharp end toward the smaller number.

senses.definition: Not discouraged or frightened by difficulty, danger, or setbacks.

history.etymology_note: A hybrid formation using the negative 'un-' plus 'daunt' (to tame). It signifies a spirit that refuses to be 'tamed' or subdued by fear.

senses.definition: Staying calm and in control when other people would get upset.

history.etymology_note: A modern English formation. 'Flap' was slang for a state of agitation; to be 'unflappable' is to be immune to those sudden flutters of panic.

senses.definition: Not pulling back from something hard, painful, or demanding.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'un-' and 'flinch' (to shrink back). It implies a physical and moral steadiness that looks a challenge straight in the eye.

senses.definition: Strong, dependable, and loyal in a way that others can rely on.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'stalworth' (stout, strong). It originally described a sturdy foundation or frame, later shifting to strong character.

senses.definition: Impossible to defeat, discourage, or control by force.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'indomitus' (untamed). In English, it evolved from describing wild beasts to describing an unconquerable human spirit.

senses.definition: Impossible to avoid, escape, or get around.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'ineluctabilis' (impossible to struggle out of). It's used for conclusions or destinies that are logically or physically inescapable.

senses.definition: Expressed so clearly that it is easy to understand.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'perspicere' (to see through). It describes language that is so transparent and clear that the meaning is seen instantly.

senses.definition: Able to control yourself and stay committed to a goal or routine.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'disciplina' (instruction/training). A 'disciplined' person has successfully trained themselves to follow an ordered path.

senses.definition: The quality of being firmly decided and hard to turn away from a goal.

history.etymology_note: From 'resolute' (unbound). A resolute person has been 'unbound' from doubt, leaving them fixed and determined.

senses.definition: Lean, strong, and tightly built in body, style, or effort.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'sinew' (tendon). It describes a strength that is lean and flexible rather than bulky—pure cord-like toughness.

senses.definition: Able to last and stay strong through wear, strain, or hardship.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'durare' (to last). It suggests a hardness or 'tiring out' of the surroundings while the object itself remains unchanged.

senses.definition: Stubbornly resistant to control, correction, or pressure.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'refragari' (to oppose). It describes a 'breaking back' or a refusal to bend to the will of others.

senses.definition: Sensitive and responsive to subtle signals, feelings, or changes.

history.etymology_note: Musical metaphor. To be 'attuned' is to have your internal instrument calibrated to the same frequency as the signals around you.

senses.definition: Calm self-control shown in a dangerous or stressful situation.

history.etymology_note: Borrowed from French 'sang-froid' (cold blood). It describes an elite level of calm that keeps the 'blood cool' when the environment is heating up.

senses.definition: Easy confidence and steady grace in a challenging moment.

history.etymology_note: From French 'aplomb' (perpendicular position/plumb line). Just as a plumb line is perfectly straight, a person with 'aplomb' has perfect, steady balance in their manner.

senses.definition: Calm and not easily excited, upset, or distracted.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'stolidus' (heavy/dull). In chemistry and character, it suggests a dense, unshakeable state that is simply too solid to be rattled.

senses.definition: Even-tempered and not given to sudden swings of mood or reaction.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'aequabilis' (uniform/level). It denotes a temperament that is like a flat, calm sea—without the peaks and valleys of emotional volatility.

senses.definition: Calm, slow to react, and not easily stirred emotionally.

history.etymology_note: From Greek roots tied to ancient medicine. It describes a cool, sluggish (but steady) nature that is immune to fiery outbursts.

senses.definition: Showing steady, careful, and persistent attention to work or duty.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'sedere' (to sit). A 'sedulous' worker is one who literally 'sits' with their task until it is done—pure dedication.

senses.definition: Completely focused on one goal or purpose without distraction.

history.etymology_note: A literal English compound for a mind that is 'single' or 'united' in its direction, rather than scattered or divided.

senses.definition: Carefully attentive to signs, details, or warnings.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'hedan' (to protect/observe). To be heedful is to be full of 'watchful care' for your path.

senses.definition: Not paying enough attention to danger, detail, or consequences.

history.etymology_note: The negative counterpart to 'heedful'. It describes a lack of 'guarding' or care in one's observation of reality.

senses.definition: So unusual or heightened that it seems beyond what is normal.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'praeter' (beyond) + 'natura' (nature). It is used for skills or events that are extraordinary and seemingly outside the usual laws of fate.

senses.definition: Strength of spirit shown in the way a person faces pressure or challenge.

history.etymology_note: A spelling variant of 'metal'. Just as the quality of a sword is in its metal, the quality of a person is in their 'mettle'—their inner durability.

senses.definition: Full of energy, courage, and spirited force.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'mettle'. It describes a person or animal (often a high-spirited horse) with lively courage and vigor.

senses.definition: Firm, loyal, and unwavering in support or conviction.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'estanche' (watertight). Like a hull that doesn't leak, a 'staunch' ally is one whose loyalty has no cracks or weak points.

senses.definition: Not turning aside from a path, purpose, or principle.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'swerve' (to turn aside). It denotes a laser-like focus that refuses to be distracted or pushed off its lane.

senses.definition: Fully concentrated on what you are doing or trying to achieve.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'intendere' (to stretch toward). It describes the mind literally 'stretching' itself toward a specific goal or observation.

senses.definition: Completely absorbed and focused in attention or feeling.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'raptus' (seized). To be 'rapt' is to be 'carried away' or 'seized' by a subject or beautiful thing—total immersion.

senses.definition: Deeply focused so that other things fade into the background.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'absorbere' (to swallow up). It is a state where the task at hand has completely 'swallowed' your attention.

senses.definition: Very sharp in noticing, understanding, or seeing beneath the surface.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'penetrare' (to enter inward). It describes a mind that 'goes inside' a problem rather than just skating on the surface.

senses.definition: To stop yourself from saying or doing something.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'refrener' (to bridle/rein in). It is the act of putting a 'rein' on your own impulses.

senses.definition: Able to feel, sense, and respond consciously.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'sentire' (to feel/perceive). It identifies the basic ability to have subjective experiences and 'feel' the world.

senses.definition: Unbreakably firm in strength, will, or resolve.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'adamas' (diamond/hardest steel). It describes a willpower or material that simply cannot be broken or cut.

senses.definition: Not made afraid or discouraged by danger or difficulty.

history.etymology_note: Built from 'daunt' (to subdue). A dauntless person is one who 'cannot be cowed' or reduced by threat.

senses.definition: Brave, tough, and strong in the face of hardship.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'dohtig' (valiant). It is one of the oldest words for a 'worthy' warrior—someone with both strength and grit.

senses.definition: Showing bold courage and determination in difficulty or danger.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'valere' (to be strong/be worth). It combines physical bravery with the 'worth' of an honorable spirit.

senses.definition: Able to endure strain, weather, hardship, or challenge without breaking down.

history.etymology_note: From Germanic-rooted Old French 'hardi' (bold). In English, its sense shifted toward durability—the ability to 'last' through winter or war.

senses.definition: Showing spirited courage even when the odds are hard.

history.etymology_note: A metaphorical shift from 'pluck' (meaning to pull out innards). In the 1800s, 'pluck' became slang for 'guts' or inner nerve.

senses.definition: Continuing with effort and purpose even when progress is slow or hard.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'perseverare' (to persist). It suggests a long-game strategy—not just a burst of effort, but a steady, unyielding climb.

senses.definition: Very sharp, quick, and precise in noticing or understanding.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'acutus' (sharp/pointed). It describes a mind that is like a needle—sharp enough to 'pierce' through confusion to find the truth.

senses.definition: Quick to notice meaning, feeling, or detail that others may miss.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'percepere' (to take in/seize). A perceptive person 'seizes' on signals and nuances that others simply don't register.

senses.definition: Careful to notice what is happening around you or within a situation.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'observare' (to watch/attend to). It is the foundational skill of taking in data from the environment with intentional focus.

senses.definition: Very careful to act correctly and pay close attention to detail.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'scrupulus' (a small sharp stone). Metaphorically, a scrupulous person feels the 'sharp stone' of a tiny mistake in their shoes—they cannot ignore details.

senses.definition: Governed by care, responsibility, and the desire to do things well and rightly.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'conscientia' (inward knowledge). It is effort guided by an internal sense of 'doing it right,' regardless of who is watching.

senses.definition: A furry animal that flies at night and uses sound to find its way.
A long wooden or metal stick used to hit a ball in baseball, cricket, or similar games.

history.etymology_note: From Middle English 'bakke', a name for the night-flying mammal of uncertain Scandinavian origin.

senses.definition: A long, snake-like fish that lives in water.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'ǣl', the same word in many old Germanic languages for this snake-like fish.

senses.definition: A very large deer with wide, branching antlers.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'eolh', related to other Germanic words for large deer.

senses.definition: A wild animal with red-orange fur, pointed ears, and a bushy tail.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'fox', unchanged in form for over a thousand years.

senses.definition: A female chicken that lays eggs.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'henn', the feminine form of 'hana' meaning rooster.

senses.definition: A bird with large round eyes that hunts at night.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'ūle', imitative of the bird's hooting call.

senses.definition: A small rodent with a long, thin tail.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'ræt', shared with other Germanic languages.

senses.definition: A graceful forest animal with thin legs, often with antlers.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'dēor', which originally meant any wild animal before narrowing to the antlered ruminant.

senses.definition: A farm animal with horns and a beard that loves to climb.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'gāt', meaning she-goat, with cognates throughout the Germanic languages.

senses.definition: A baby sheep with soft, woolly fur.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'lamb', the same form in Old High German and Old Norse.

senses.definition: A small furry animal that digs tunnels underground.

history.etymology_note: From Middle English 'molle', possibly related to mold or the verb to grind, since moles burrow through soil.

senses.definition: A night insect that looks like a butterfly with duller wings.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'moððe', name for the winged insect, related to similar words across Germanic languages.

senses.definition: A sleek ocean mammal with flippers, found on rocky shores.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'seolh', the marine mammal, an ancient Germanic word.

senses.definition: A large, graceful white water bird with a long, curved neck.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'swan', unchanged since the early Middle Ages.

senses.definition: A hopping animal like a frog with bumpy, dry skin.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'tāde' or 'tādige', of uncertain origin but used in English for over a thousand years.

senses.definition: A long, soft creature with no legs that wiggles through dirt.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'wyrm', which originally meant any serpent or dragon before narrowing to the soft burrowing creature.

senses.definition: A big water bird with a long neck and a loud honk.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'gōs', shared with Old High German 'gans' and Old Norse 'gás'.

senses.definition: A tiny rodent with round ears and a long thin tail.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'mūs', an ancient word shared across Indo-European languages, including Latin 'mus'.

senses.definition: A tiny round green vegetable that grows inside a pod.

history.etymology_note: Back-formed from the older English word 'pease', which was thought to be plural, from Latin 'pisum'.

senses.definition: A hard-shelled snack that grows on trees and is full of seeds.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'hnutu', shared with Old Norse 'hnot' and other Germanic languages.

senses.definition: A sweet, sticky fruit spread you put on toast.
A traffic backup where cars are stuck and cannot move forward.

history.etymology_note: From the verb 'jam', meaning to press tightly, since fruit is crushed to make the spread.

senses.definition: A baked treat with a crust and a sweet or savory filling.

history.etymology_note: Possibly named after the magpie, whose habit of collecting random things resembled the mix of fillings in early pies.

senses.definition: A warm drink made by soaking leaves in hot water.

history.etymology_note: From Min Nan Chinese 'tê', brought to Europe by Dutch traders. The word followed the spread of the drink.

senses.definition: Salty meat that comes from a pig.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'hamm', originally meaning the back of the knee or thigh, and later the cured meat from that part of a pig.

senses.definition: A soft, sweet fruit with tiny seeds inside.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'ficus', through Old French 'figue', for the soft sweet fruit grown around the Mediterranean.

senses.definition: A small, round bread roll, often with sugar or fruit inside.

history.etymology_note: From Middle English 'bunne', possibly from Old French 'bugne' meaning a swelling or lump.

senses.definition: A small seed used for food, growing inside a long green pod.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'bēan', an ancient Germanic word for the protein-rich seed.

senses.definition: A white drink that comes from cows, goats, and other mammals.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'meoluc', meaning milk, with cognates across the Germanic languages.

senses.definition: Small white grains that we cook and eat as food.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'oryza' through Latin and Old French, reaching English in the Middle Ages as the grain spread through Europe.

senses.definition: A hot liquid meal often with vegetables, meat, or noodles.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'soupe', meaning broth poured over bread. Related to 'sop' in English.

senses.definition: A sweet, juicy fruit shaped like a teardrop.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'pirum' through Old English 'peru', for the soft sweet fruit related to the apple.

senses.definition: A small green sour fruit related to the lemon.

history.etymology_note: From Arabic 'līma' through Spanish and French, naming the small green citrus fruit.

senses.definition: A small purple fruit with a pit inside.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'prunum' through Old English 'plūme', for the smooth-skinned stone fruit.

senses.definition: A sweet, sticky food that bees make from flower nectar.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'hunig', shared across the Germanic languages, the oldest sweetener used by humans.

senses.definition: A bright yellow sour fruit.

history.etymology_note: From Arabic 'līmūn' through Old French 'limon', for the yellow citrus fruit.

senses.definition: A small green or black fruit used to make oil.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'oliva' through Old French, the fruit of the olive tree native to the Mediterranean.

senses.definition: A round, fuzzy, sweet fruit with a pit inside.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'persicum', meaning 'Persian apple', through Old French 'pesche'.

senses.definition: A small, round, sweet fruit that grows in bunches on a vine.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'grape', meaning a cluster, possibly from a Germanic root meaning to hook or pick.

senses.definition: A big, sweet fruit with juicy flesh inside a thick rind.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'mēlopepōn', meaning 'apple-shaped gourd', shortened through Latin and Old French.

senses.definition: A very large body of salty water.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'sǣ', a core Germanic word for a large body of water.

senses.definition: The invisible gas all around us that we breathe.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'aēr' through Latin 'aer' and Old French 'air', meaning the atmosphere we breathe.

senses.definition: A thick cloud close to the ground that makes it hard to see.

history.etymology_note: Likely from a Scandinavian source related to Danish 'fog' meaning spray or shower.

senses.definition: Tiny drops of water that form on grass and leaves in the morning.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'tima' meaning a limited space of time, related to 'tide'.

senses.definition: What a person, place, or thing is called.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'nama', shared across the Germanic languages, related to Latin 'nomen'.

senses.definition: An activity with rules that people play for fun.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'gamen' meaning joy or sport.

senses.definition: One movement of your foot when walking.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'stæpe', a core Germanic word for a footstep.

senses.definition: To halt or come to an end.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'stoppian' meaning to plug or close up.

senses.definition: A journey to somewhere, usually short.

history.etymology_note: From Middle Dutch 'trippen' meaning to step or tread lightly, evolving to mean a journey.

senses.definition: To let something fall.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'droppian', related to 'drop' (a small bit of liquid).

senses.definition: A long thin sticky strip used to join things together.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'tæppe' meaning a band or ribbon.

senses.definition: To do something useful for another person.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'helpan', a core Germanic verb of supporting others.

senses.definition: The food eaten at one time, like breakfast or dinner.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'mæl' meaning a measure of time, including the times at which one eats.

senses.definition: What people and animals eat to stay alive.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'foda' meaning food, fodder, or nourishment.

senses.definition: A group of items written down, one after another.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'liste' meaning a strip or border, later coming to mean an enumerated series.

senses.definition: Coming after all others; final.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'latost' meaning latest, from 'læt' meaning slow or late.

senses.definition: Better than all others.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'betst', the superlative form of 'good', a core Germanic word.

senses.definition: A particular space or region of the world or a building.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'area' meaning a level piece of ground.

senses.definition: A thin strip used to hold things together, or a group of musicians.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'bande' meaning a strip or troop, with both meanings developing in English.

senses.definition: A public open space with grass and trees where people can play and relax.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'parc' meaning an enclosed land for hunting, evolving to mean public green space.

senses.definition: The long part at the back of an animal's body.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'tægel' meaning the hindmost part of an animal.

senses.definition: A large container for holding liquids or gas.

history.etymology_note: From Portuguese 'tanque' meaning a pond or reservoir, originally from Sanskrit 'tadaga'.

senses.definition: A group of letters with a meaning, used in speaking and writing.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'word', a core Indo-European word for speech-unit.

senses.definition: To move something away from you by pressing on it.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'pulsare' meaning to strike or push, through Old French 'pousser'.

senses.definition: To move something toward you by tugging on it.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'pullian' meaning to pluck or tug.

senses.definition: To make something no longer closed.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'openian', from 'open' meaning not closed.

senses.definition: To raise something up to a higher place.

history.etymology_note: From Old Norse 'lypta' meaning to raise up, brought to English by Norse settlers.

senses.definition: To have something in your hands.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'healdan' meaning to keep, contain, or grasp.

senses.definition: To keep something safe, or to rescue someone from danger.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'salvare' meaning to make safe, through Old French 'sauver'.

senses.definition: To sit on or in something that moves and travel along with it.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'ridan', a core Germanic verb for traveling on horseback or vehicle.

senses.definition: A small flat piece of stiff paper used for messages, games, or playing.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'khartes' meaning papyrus leaf, through Latin 'carta' and Old French 'carte'.

senses.definition: One side of a sheet of paper in a book.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'pagina' meaning a written page or column of writing.

senses.definition: A separate space inside a building, with walls and a floor.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'rum' meaning open space or room.

senses.definition: Something given to someone to show love or celebration.

history.etymology_note: From Old Norse 'gift' meaning something given, related to the verb 'give'.

senses.definition: A baked food made from flour, water, and yeast.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'bread', originally meaning a small piece of food, narrowing to the baked loaf.

senses.definition: A sweet drink made from squeezed fruit.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'jus' meaning broth or sauce, through Old French 'jus' meaning liquid.

senses.definition: A living thing with roots, leaves, and stems that grows in soil.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'planta' meaning a young shoot or sprout, used in Old English for any vegetation.

senses.definition: A gathering where people celebrate with food, games, and friends.

history.etymology_note: From Latin 'partita' meaning a part or share, evolving through Old French 'partie' to mean a gathered group.

senses.definition: A woman who rules a country, or the wife of a king.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'cwen' meaning a woman or wife, narrowing to mean a female ruler.

senses.definition: A sweet food made mostly of sugar.

history.etymology_note: From Arabic 'qandi' meaning made of sugar, through Persian 'qand' meaning cane sugar.

senses.definition: Special powers that seem to make impossible things happen.

history.etymology_note: From Greek 'magikos', referring to the Magi, ancient priest-magicians of Persia.

senses.definition: A thin stick with a sharp point, shot from a bow.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'arwe' meaning a shaft shot from a bow.

senses.definition: A covering for the hand with separate spaces for each finger.

history.etymology_note: From Old English 'glof' meaning a covering for the hand.

senses.definition: A long piece of cloth worn around the neck for warmth or style.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'escharpe' meaning a pilgrim's pouch hung from the neck, later a neck cloth.

senses.definition: To use your nose to notice an odor.

history.etymology_note: From Middle English 'smellen', of uncertain origin but a core Germanic verb.

senses.definition: To put a little of something in your mouth to see what it is like.

history.etymology_note: From Old French 'taster' meaning to feel or touch, narrowing in English to mean perceiving flavor.
